Keywords: partition count, topic partitions, parallelism, rebalance cost
Guidance: Under-partitioning a topic caps consumer parallelism (partitions are the unit of parallel consumption), while over-partitioning inflates rebalance time and per-partition overhead across brokers.
Do: Size partition count based on target throughput divided by per-partition throughput, leaving headroom for consumer scale-out, not an arbitrary round number.
Don't: Pick partition count arbitrarily (e.g. always 3) with no relation to expected throughput or consumer parallelism.

Guidance: Frequent consumer restarts or pod churn (common in Kubernetes with aggressive HPA) trigger repeated stop-the-world rebalances under the eager protocol, stalling the whole group during each one.
Do: Use the cooperative-sticky partition assignor and tune session.timeout.ms/max.poll.interval.ms to reduce unnecessary rebalances from transient pod churn.
Don't: Use the default eager rebalance protocol on a consumer group with frequent pod restarts/autoscaling.

Guidance: A replication factor of 1 (or min.insync.replicas=1 with acks=all) means a single broker failure can lose committed data; production topics need both a real replication factor and matched ISR requirements.
Do: Set replication.factor >= 3 and min.insync.replicas=2 for production topics that can't tolerate data loss.
Don't: Run production topics with replication.factor=1 or min.insync.replicas=1.

Guidance: Leaving retention at the cluster default (often 7 days, delete policy) on a topic meant as a durable changelog silently loses old keys' state; compacted topics need cleanup.policy=compact instead.
Do: Set retention.ms/retention.bytes deliberately per topic's actual use case, and use cleanup.policy=compact for changelog-style topics.
Don't: Leave every topic on the cluster-wide default retention regardless of its actual data lifecycle needs.

Keywords: acks, producer durability, fire and forget
Guidance: acks=0 (fire-and-forget) or acks=1 (leader-only ack) can silently lose messages on broker failure right after the ack is sent; acks=all is required for durability guarantees.
Do: Use acks=all with min.insync.replicas for any producer where message loss is unacceptable.
Don't: Use acks=0 or acks=1 for producers writing business-critical events.

Guidance: Without idempotence enabled, a producer retry after a transient network error can write the same message twice, and downstream consumers see duplicates unless they dedupe themselves.
Do: Enable enable.idempotence=true (default in modern clients) so retries don't create duplicate messages at the broker level.
Don't: Disable idempotence on a producer that retries on failure, relying entirely on downstream dedup logic.

Keywords: consumer lag, offset lag, kafka lag exporter
Guidance: Without consumer lag monitoring, a consumer that's silently falling behind (or stuck) looks identical to a healthy one until downstream data staleness becomes a customer-visible incident.
Do: Monitor consumer group lag per partition (via Burrow, kafka-lag-exporter, or kafka-consumer-groups.sh) with alerting on sustained growth.
Don't: Run consumer groups in production with no lag monitoring or alerting configured.

Guidance: Ad-hoc topic names with no convention (env, domain, entity, version) make it impossible to apply consistent ACLs, retention policies, or ownership at scale once a cluster has hundreds of topics.
Do: Adopt a consistent naming convention (e.g. env.domain.entity.version) so ACLs, retention, and ownership tooling can pattern-match topics.
Don't: Let teams name topics arbitrarily with no shared convention as the cluster grows.

Keywords: kraft, zookeeper, controller quorum, metadata mode
Guidance: ZooKeeper-based clusters are on a deprecation path and carry an extra distributed system to operate; new clusters should run KRaft mode with a dedicated controller quorum instead.
Do: Deploy new Kafka clusters in KRaft mode; plan a migration off ZooKeeper for existing clusters before it's removed.
Don't: Stand up a brand-new production Kafka cluster on ZooKeeper mode in 2026.

Topic: Static group membership for stable assignment
Keywords: group.instance.id, static membership, rolling restart rebalance
Guidance: Without static membership, every rolling restart of a consumer deployment triggers a full rebalance because each pod rejoins as a 'new' consumer instance.
Do: Set group.instance.id per consumer instance so rolling restarts are treated as temporary absences, not membership changes, avoiding unnecessary rebalances.
Don't: Roll consumer deployments with no group.instance.id set, triggering a full rebalance on every deploy.

Topic: Broker disk and page cache sizing
Keywords: page cache, sequential io, broker disk, log segment
Guidance: Kafka's performance relies heavily on OS page cache for sequential reads/writes; undersized broker memory (relative to hot data) forces disk reads that dramatically increase consumer fetch latency.
Do: Size broker memory so the working set (recent log segments actively being read) fits in page cache, not just JVM heap.
Don't: Size Kafka broker memory based only on JVM heap needs, ignoring page cache requirements for the actual log data.
Example: # heap ~6GB, remaining RAM left for OS page cache on a 32GB broker

Guidance: Running a cluster with authorization disabled (or overly permissive ACLs) lets any client with network access produce/consume any topic, including ones holding sensitive data.
Do: Enable an authorizer and grant per-principal ACLs scoped to the specific topics/consumer groups each client needs.
Don't: Run a shared multi-team Kafka cluster with no authorizer or ACLs configured.
